paragraph: Meet the physical manuscripts behind the printed Bible. Examine what remains, follow where it travelled, and learn to see the difference between evidence and inference.

blocks.text: The words reached us. The pages did not all survive.
Meet the physical manuscripts behind the printed Bible. Examine what remains, follow where it travelled, and learn to see the difference between evidence and inference.
Six witnesses. Six ways to look.
Select a manuscript to examine it. This is a selection, not a census.
Photograph · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons (opens in a new tab)
A complete New Testament. An incomplete Bible.
Sinaiticus preserves the whole New Testament, alongside an incomplete Old Testament and other early Christian writings.
The surviving codex has over 400 large parchment leaves. Its pages are material evidence of the work of scribes, correctors and the people who preserved it.
British Library, London Leipzig University Library St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai National Library of Russia, St Petersburg
“Complete” needs an object: the whole New Testament survives, but large parts of the Old Testament do not. Neither description should be stretched to cover the other.

Not one book of the Bible survives in its author’s own hand. What we have are copies, and copies of copies, in more languages and from more centuries than any other ancient text. These are the open records behind this site’s collection.
262 of them hold a book of the Bible. Beside them, 220 Hebrew codices and 3 Samaritan Pentateuchs.
The Septuagint, the Bible of the first Greek-speaking churches. Only 75 of these records carry a date.
1,809 have an open record here, among them 134 of the 141 papyri.
Latin, Syriac, Armenian, Slavonic, Arabic, Georgian, Coptic, Gothic and Ge’ez. The real numbers are far larger: Latin copies alone run to thousands.
The 3,115 records that carry a date, by century. The scrolls end with the first century; the Greek papyri begin in the second; most copies of everything are mediaeval. Point at a century to count it.
The gap between author and oldest copy.

For each New Testament book: when it was written, as a wide approximate range that holds the main scholarly views, and the oldest copy in the open data that holds it. Most early copies are dated by their handwriting, so their dates are estimates too. For most ancient books the gap is many centuries; for several New Testament books it is a few generations.
Point at a book to read its oldest copy here; choose it to open the record.
Count what remains. Notice what is missing.
P46 makes survival tangible. Each small leaf here stands for one leaf in Michigan’s account of the codex.
A surviving leaf need not be intact. Lost lines within these leaves mean that a leaf count is not a percentage of readable text.
One symbol = one leaf, with two sides. Grouped by present custody; this is not the original leaf order. The 104-leaf total is a reconstruction reported by Michigan.
Scattered like P46, across three continents.

2,042 records name a library we can place on a map: 68 libraries, museums and monasteries in 53 cities. The largest keepers are national and university libraries that gathered manuscripts from the eastern Mediterranean over the last five centuries.

5,269 open records through time and book by book, the great witnesses on one shelf, and the libraries that keep them on a map.
